Daniel’s equation—“*Baba Is You* = 缘起性空 (dependent origination / emptiness)”—is evocative, but in its current “RT” form it mostly gestures rather than argues. The game does dramatize a core Madhyamaka insight: what a thing *is* depends on relations and conventions (here, rule-statements like “BABA IS YOU”), not on an intrinsic essence. Yet the post skips the key step Nāgārjuna forces on any such analogy: showing *how* conventional re-description avoids collapsing into either “nothing is real” (nihilism) or “the rules are the hidden reality” (a new essentialism). Without that, “emptiness” becomes a poetic synonym for “everything is mutable,” which is weaker than the Buddhist claim that essences fail *because* things arise dependently and only function within a web of conditions (see [Nāgārjuna / *Mulamadhyamakakarika*](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/nagarjuna/)).

There’s also a quiet blind spot in mapping a rule-based puzzle world onto a soteriological doctrine. In *Baba Is You*, the rules are explicit, enumerable, and often under the player’s control; in dependent origination, the “rules” are not a manipulable syntax but an account of causality, cognition, and suffering—ethics and attention matter, not just re-labeling. If Daniel wants the analogy to do real work, he might name the asymmetry: the game is a clean laboratory for *conceptual dependence* (how categories govern action), whereas 缘起 includes *existential dependence* (how craving and ignorance condition experience). That distinction would keep the comparison from implying that insight is merely a clever reframing.

A richer expansion would be to connect the game not only to Buddhism but also to a Western lineage that treats meaning as use and rules as practices: Wittgenstein’s later philosophy, where “grammar” determines what can be said and done, often invisibly ([*Philosophical Investigations*](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/wittgenstein/#LatePhil)). *Baba Is You* makes the grammar visible and editable; Madhyamaka argues that ordinary grammar looks “natural” only because we forget its dependence. Framed that way, Daniel’s comparison becomes more than a meme: it becomes a clear lesson about how worlds—game-worlds and lived worlds—are constructed by the rules we inherit, and the price we pay when we mistake those rules for essence.
